title: The Misls close
hookLine: twelve bands of equals, and the beginnings of a kingdom

cards: Lay the banners out side by side. The Bhangi, strong for a time. The Ahluwalia, the leader's band.
The Ramgarhia, the builders. The Kanhaiya, where Sada Kaur rose. The Sukerchakia, small beginnings.
The Nakai, named for its land. The Dallewalia by the river. The Nishanwalia, carrying the flag.
The Singhpuria, the nawab's band. The Karorsinghia of the Doaba. The Shaheedan, the martyrs' band.

teach.b: Step back and the block has a shape. It began with an idea: a misl was a band of equals with its own chief, joined to the others in the Dal Khalsa. No band owned the others, and riders could follow a chief they trusted.
When something had to be decided for everyone, the bands rode to Amritsar at Vaisakhi and Diwali, sat as the Sarbat Khalsa before the Guru Granth Sahib, and agreed a gurmata that bound them all.
Around the sacred pool they built bungas, rest for pilgrims and posts for defenders, and towers that still stand. That's the first movement: equals, sharing a center. The second is the strain.
When the danger faded, the bands turned on each other over land and pride, and the gatherings grew harder to hold together. The third is where the block ends.

Inside one band, a boy has just become chief. He is promised to the daughter of a woman who leads a misl of her own and has put her riders behind him, and he has a world of quarreling equals around him.
The next part of this path follows what he did with it.
The histories call him Maharaja Ranjit Singh.
Sikhs remember his reign in more than one way: as a high point of Sikh rule, and as the moment the bands of equals became a kingdom. Both are part of the story.

how: Sikh histories tell the misl period as the time the Sikh bands held Punjab as confederacies of equals, before Maharaja Ranjit Singh brought them under one rule.

o: a Sikh band of equals with its own chief
a royal house that passed down a family line
a rest-house built beside the sacred pool

games.q: the misls, end to end — tap the pairs.
p: a band of equals with its own chief
the whole Khalsa, meeting at Amritsar

the misls decided shared matters before the Guru Granth Sahib at Amritsar

as danger faded, rivalry grew between them.

games.q: you're a rider in a band of equals. the old enemy is weaker, the chiefs are quarreling, and a young chief is rising. what comes next in the story?
o: the misls dissolve and the riders go home.
the bands of equals give way to a kingdom.
an outside ruler takes all of Punjab at once.
games.why: the next block follows the boy of the Sukerchakia misl, Ranjit Singh, as the bands of equals become a kingdom.

practice: Bring to mind a group you're part of, a family, a crew at work, a congregation, and remember a hard stretch it came through together.

Then look at it now, when things are easier, and notice without judging whether it still pulls the same way, and what might help it hold together when nothing presses it; if you pray, Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: misl, a band of equals with its own chief. This block: what a misl was, the banners, twice a year at Amritsar, the bungas, the towers, the quarrels, Rani Sada Kaur, and a boy of twelve. Today's word.
